lesson.title: The Nervous System's Middlemen
lesson.summary: Interneurons connect other neurons entirely within the central nervous system, and because they make up the vast majority of the brain's neurons, they form the basis for complex processing between raw sensory input and final motor output.
lesson.body:
Sensory neurons carry information in and motor neurons carry commands out, but neither type talks directly to the other in most circuits. That job belongs to interneurons, neurons that live entirely within the central nervous system and connect other neurons to each other, whether that means linking a sensory neuron to a motor neuron, or linking thousands of neurons within the brain to one another.

Interneurons are not a minor category. The overwhelming majority of neurons in the human nervous system are interneurons rather than sensory or motor neurons. This makes sense once you consider what most of the nervous system actually does: relatively little of it is dedicated to raw sensory input or final motor output, while the vast bulk of it is devoted to processing, comparing, storing, and combining information between those two endpoints. Nearly all of what we call thought, memory, and decision-making happens in networks of interneurons within the brain.

Because interneurons can receive input from many sources and send output to many targets, they allow the nervous system to do far more than simply relay signals unchanged. A single interneuron might combine information from several sensory neurons before deciding whether to pass a signal on, or it might inhibit one motor pathway while exciting another, allowing coordinated rather than chaotic responses. Many interneurons, especially in the cerebral cortex, release the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA rather than an excitatory one, which dampens the activity of neighboring neurons instead of exciting them. This balance between excitatory and inhibitory interneurons keeps neural circuits from either falling silent or firing out of control, supporting the kind of stable, fine-tuned processing that complex behavior requires.

The withdrawal reflex described in earlier sections offers a clear example. When a sensory neuron detects a painful stimulus, it does not usually connect straight to a motor neuron. Instead it typically synapses onto an interneuron in the spinal cord's gray matter, which then excites the motor neuron that contracts the withdrawing muscle while simultaneously inhibiting the motor neuron that would contract the opposing muscle, a pattern called reciprocal inhibition that lets the limb pull away smoothly instead of fighting itself. A separate branch from that same interneuron network relays the signal up toward the brain, so the reflex and the conscious experience of pain can happen almost simultaneously through parallel pathways.

Interneurons matter functionally because they are what make the nervous system a processing system rather than a simple wire. Without them, sensory input could only ever trigger fixed, hardwired motor responses, and the flexible, learned, context-sensitive behavior that defines complex nervous systems, including the human capacity for reasoning and memory, would not be possible.
